sources.entry: Code rant: The Configuration Complexity Clock

summary.title: The Configuration Complexity Clock
summary.one_liner: Configuration tends to grow from hard-coded values through config files and rules engines to a DSL, and past a certain complexity hard-coding may be the least bad option.
takeaways: Configuration usually escalates in stages: hard-coded values, flat config files, structured XML, a database-backed rules engine, then a custom DSL.
Each stage adds complexity, bugs and learning curve, and the team can end up needing rare skills to change configuration.
At a certain level of complexity, hard-coding a solution may be the least evil option, especially with a fast build-test-deploy cycle.
Before building a rules engine or DSL, understand the implications and where your system sits on the clock.
summary.summary: Mike Hadlow describes a 'Configuration Complexity Clock' as an extended anecdote in which a simple application's hard-coded values move into config files, then XML schemas, then a business rules engine, then a custom DSL, and eventually the team is back to hard coding in a worse language. He argues that past a point, configuration complexity causes more pain than it solves. The piece is opinion and experience rather than a technical tutorial, and it does not include code or specific tools beyond the mentioned rules engine and DSL.
